title: Memory tricks (mnemonics)
keyIdea: A mnemonic is a memory trick that holds a list in the right order. In a first-letter sentence, each word starts with the same letter as the thing you want, so Richard Of York Gave Battle In Vain gives red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. A rhyme such as Thirty days has September uses rhythm to hold a list, and a spelling sentence such as Big Elephants Can Always Understand Small Elephants fixes the tricky letters in because. The trick only gives you a cue: you still have to know the words it stands for, and it does not explain why anything is true.

kid: A mnemonic is a memory trick. It helps you remember a list in the right order.
One kind is a silly sentence. Each word starts with the same letter as a thing on your list. Richard Of York Gave Battle In Vain gives the rainbow: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.

Rhymes work too. Thirty days has September, April, June and November tells you the four months with 30 days. A sentence can fix a spelling: Big Elephants Can Always Understand Small Elephants spells because.

But the trick only gives the first letter. My Very Easy Method gives two M words, and only your planet facts tell you that Mercury comes before Mars. Learn the list first. Then use the trick to keep it in order.
adult: This is part of learning to learn. Children choose a memory trick that fits the job. The EEF guide on metacognition says: teach each strategy out loud, and show when to use it. In England, children meet first-letter tricks for the rainbow, the planets and the compass. They meet spelling tricks for Year 3 and 4 words such as because.

Why it works: a list with no pattern is hard to hold. A trick turns it into one short story with a beat. Each first letter is a cue that brings back a word you know. Reviews of the research (Bellezza 1981; Dunlosky and others 2013) say tricks help most with lists in order. They help little with understanding. The old planet sentence ended with Pizzas for Pluto. Pluto has been a dwarf planet since 2006.

Common mistakes to watch for. A child thinks the trick holds the answer, so if they never learned indigo they are stuck at I. They pick a word with the right letter but put it in the wrong place. They mix up two things with the same letter, such as Mercury and Mars. Be careful not to use a trick where a reason is needed. After the trick, have them say the list and check it.

In the lab your child decodes the rainbow sentence. They find that the planet sentence only works with planet facts. They build a sentence for North, East, South, West and use the rhyme to pick months. Then they spell because. Each wrong tap gets a note that names the slip.

familyTip: Make up a silly sentence together for something your child needs to learn in order, such as the days of the week or a tricky spelling. The sillier the better. Tomorrow, ask them to say the sentence and then the list it stands for.

visual.caption: Which kind of memory trick is it? Drag each one, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Richard Of York Gave Battle In Vain
Thirty days has September, April, June and November
In fourteen hundred and ninety-two, Columbus sailed the ocean blue
ROY G BIV for the rainbow
FANBOYS for for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so

lab.caption: Flagship lab: decode the rainbow and planet sentences, build your own for the compass, use a rhyme for the months and spell because.

practice.prompt: In Richard Of York Gave Battle In Vain, which colour does Battle stand for?
practice.hint: Only rainbow colours are in the list. Which one starts with B?
practice.explain: Battle gives B, and the only rainbow colour starting with B is blue.

practice.prompt: You make a first-letter sentence for a list of {n} things. How many words should the sentence have?
practice.hint: Each word gives the first letter of one thing on the list.
practice.explain: One word for each thing, so the sentence has {n} words.

practice.prompt: The planets sentence has 8 words. You can name {k} planets from it. How many more do you still need?
practice.hint: Take the planets you know from the 8 in the sentence.
practice.explain: 8 take away {k} leaves {=8-k} planets still to learn.

practice.prompt: My Very Easy Method gives two M words. How do you know the first M is Mercury, not Mars?
choices: You need to know Mercury is closest to the Sun
practice.hint: Does the letter M tell you which M planet it is?
practice.explain: The trick only gives the letter. Your planet facts tell you Mercury comes first.

pool.hint: Say the rhyme: Thirty days has September, April, June and November.
pool.explain: June is in the rhyme, so it has 30 days. July and August have 31.

pool.prompt: Big Elephants Can Always Understand Small Elephants spells which word?
pool.hint: Write down the first letter of each word, in order.
pool.explain: B-E-C-A-U-S-E. Always comes before Understand, so it is a then u.

pool.prompt: Which sentence helps you remember North, East, South, West in that order?
pool.hint: Check the first letter of each word against N, E, S, W.
pool.explain: Never Eat Shredded Wheat gives N, E, S, W in the right order.

pool.prompt: A friend learns Richard Of York Gave Battle In Vain but has never heard of indigo. What happens at In?
choices: They are stuck: the trick only gives I
pool.hint: What does each word of the sentence give you?
pool.explain: A mnemonic is only a cue. If you never learned indigo, the letter I cannot bring it back.

pool.prompt: A first-letter sentence has {w} words. You remember the first {k} of them. How many words are left to remember?
pool.hint: Take the words you remember from all the words in the sentence.
pool.explain: {w} take away {k} leaves {=w-k} words still to remember.

pool.prompt: When does a mnemonic help most?
choices: Understanding why the sky is blue
Solving a new kind of puzzle
pool.hint: A mnemonic holds letters, not reasons.
pool.explain: Mnemonics hold lists in order. Understanding why needs explaining and thinking.

pool.prompt: What is the best way to check your mnemonic worked?
choices: Say the list from memory, then check it
pool.hint: How do you find out if you can really remember something?
pool.explain: Test yourself: say the whole list from the trick, then check it against the real list.

pool.prompt: ROY G BIV stands for 7 rainbow colours. You have said {s} of them. How many colours are left to say?
pool.hint: Take the colours you have said from the 7 in the rainbow.
pool.explain: 7 take away {s} leaves {=7-s} colours still to say.
